entry.title: Comparison of entangling strategies for unitary synthesis
entry.summary: Trapped-ion quantum computers are promising as a platform for realizing quantum computational advantage. They promise long coherence times, near all-to-all connectivity, and potential multiqubit gates as distinguishing advantages compared to competing platforms. Regarding these advantages, it is crucial to understand the trade-offs between increasing engineering complexity and actual improvements in running quantum algorithms with a more flexible gate set. In this work, we investigate this question and develop a versatile toolset to evaluate the performance of gate sets composed of native Mølmer--Sørensen multiqubit gates. To this end, we employ unitary synthesis as an application-agnostic benchmark target and identify specific hardware requirements for multiqubit gates to be advantageous.

entry.title: Improved Gradient Complexity for Quasi-Newton Proximal Extragradient Methods via Certified Curvature Reuse
entry.summary: We study how curvature estimated from gradient differences can accelerate proximal-extragradient quasi-Newton methods. Existing global guarantees for QNPE, A-QNPE, and OL-OQN learn Hessian approximations online and incur dimension dependence through regret bounds. We introduce certified curvature reuse: one finite-difference probe per iteration refreshes a group of Hessian columns, while a path-length certificate controls the error of stale columns and determines the step. Each iteration uses at most three gradient queries and one regularized linear solve (or trust-region step), without a gradient line search or an inner oracle-querying loop. In the convex and strongly convex settings, bisection on stored scalar quantities selects a near-maximal certified stepsize; in the nonconvex setting, a uniform certificate gives an explicit learning rate. With other problem parameters fixed, the convex method attains $O(\min\{k^{-2},dk^{-3}\})$ in a single run, with no logarithmic factor or additive dimension term, matching accelerated gradient descent (AGD) for $k\lesssim d$ and improving on A-QNPE thereafter. In the strongly convex setting with condition number $κ$, a single run matches AGD's $(1-Θ(κ^{-1/2}))^k$ rate for $k\lesssim d\logκ$ and achieves a superlinear upper envelope, eventually scaling as $(1+k^2/B^2)^{-k}$ with $B=\tilde O(dκ)$, improving on QNPE. In the nonconvex setting, the method finds an $\varepsilon$-stationary point in $O(\min\{d^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-3/2},\varepsilon^{-7/4}\})$ gradient queries, improving on OL-OQN's $O(d^{1/4}\varepsilon^{-13/8})$. For sparse Hessians, $d$ is replaced by an effective dimension $χ\le d$. We also compare our bounds with lazy-Hessian, double-loop, and cutting-plane methods.

entry.title: A self-normalized law of the iterated logarithm for Rademacher random multiplicative functions
Approximating Minimum Spanning Trees in Metrics under Semi-Random Corruptions
entry.summary: We study the problem of finding minimum spanning trees in semi-random corrupted metrics. In this problem proposed by Bateni, Dharangutte, Jayaram, and Wang (COLT'24), we start with a metric space $\mathcal{M} = (X, d)$. The adversary independently corrupts each pairwise distance with probability $p$. The algorithm only observes these possibly corrupted distances and must output a spanning tree whose expected cost (in the true metric) is multiplicatively close to the minimum spanning tree cost. Prior work showed that losing a factor of $Ω(\log n)$ is necessary, even if the algorithm may adaptively select $O(n/\log n)$ points and probe the true distances between them. However, no upper bounds were known. We study three regimes based on whether the adversary can only increase, decrease, or arbitrarily change the corrupted distances. We show the following: (1) In the increase-only setting, we give a polynomial-time $O(1)$-approximation algorithm for any constant $0 \le p < 1$. (2) In the decrease-only setting, we give an $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithm for any constant $0 \le p < 1$. Additionally, we show an $O(\log^4 n)$-approximation algorithm that runs in quasi-polynomial time $n^{O(\log n)}$, for any constant $p \leq 0.1$. Moreover, we show that a polynomial-time algorithm computing an $n^{1/3-\varepsilon}$-approximation is unlikely to exist. (3) In the general setting, where the adversary can both increase and decrease distances, we show an $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithm for every $0 \leq p < \frac{1}{4}$. Further, we show that no $o(n)$-approximation is possible for $\frac{1}{2} \leq p < 1$. Our algorithms answer the main open question in Bateni et al.'s work; moreover, the $O(\log n)$-approximations in the latter two settings are information-theoretically optimal.
